article.headline: A Thin Pointer to YouTube Lectures, Context Unknown
article.lede: A brief post from @kristinelizx notes that the previous year's lectures — described as "stacked," meaning high-quality or impressively curated — are available on YouTube. The tweet reads as a follow-up to something already in progress: a thread, a recommendation list, or an ongoing discussion whose topic is not recoverable from the post alone.
article.body:
The tweet functions as a caption rather than a claim. It adds a data point — the prior year's content is archived on YouTube — but does not name the subject, course, speaker, or channel. The word *stacked*, in contemporary internet usage, signals that the material is dense with value: well-sourced, substantive, not padded.

Without the surrounding thread or a working link to the YouTube content, the specific domain of these lectures — whether mathematics, economics, computer science, or something else entirely — cannot be determined. The research sources returned no useful identifying information, and the poster's prior tweet referenced by the URL was inaccessible.

What can be said: the poster treats this as a recommendation, not a discovery. The phrasing "also stacked" implies a parallel set of current-year lectures has already been praised, and this is an addendum pointing readers toward the older archive. The recommendation is implicit but genuine.

concepts.definition: Used colloquially to mean that something is impressively dense with quality content — packed with substance, well-curated, or unusually high in value relative to expectations. It carries an endorsement: the thing described is worth your time.

article.thread_summary: This appears to be part of a longer thread or reply chain. The phrase "also stacked" strongly implies a preceding post already recommended current-year lectures; this post adds that last year's equivalent content is on YouTube. The full thread context is not recoverable from available sources.
